\chapter{Habla --- Telling Somebody To Do Something}
\label{ch:command-tu}
\hlchaptermodality{109}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can give an informal positive command using a form I already hold.}

Complete ES-C50-habla: give a tu command and name the form it reuses.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[habla · come · vive]{habla — telling somebody to do something}

\label{lesson:ES-C50-habla}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}he speaks.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Habla}.) Hold that word. You are about to be told it does a second job you have never been shown.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: you already have it}]
\begin{quote}
To tell somebody you address as \emph{tú} to do something, use the \textbf{he/she} form of the present.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Habla.} — Speak. \emph{Come.} — Eat. \emph{Vive.} — Live.
\end{quote}

That is the whole rule, and it costs you nothing. \emph{Habla} was already in your mouth as \textquotedblleft{}he speaks\textquotedblright{}; the same two syllables, said to somebody, are an order.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{verb} & \textbf{he/she does} & \textbf{you, do it} \\
\midrule
\emph{hablar} & habla & \textbf{habla} \\
\emph{comer} & come & \textbf{come} \\
\emph{vivir} & vive & \textbf{vive} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The column repeats. That is not an oversight in the table.

Spanish does this often enough that it is worth naming as a habit: rather than inventing a new form for every job, it \textbf{reuses one and lets context sort it out.} \emph{Habla} said about somebody is a statement; \emph{habla} said to somebody is a command, and nobody has ever confused the two.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
The name for this form is the \textbf{imperative}, from Latin \textbf{imperāre}, \textquotedblleft{}to command.\textquotedblright{}

That \emph{imper-} is a word you already know in English clothes. An \textbf{emperor} is literally \emph{one who commands}; an \textbf{empire} is the thing he commands. The grammar term and the political ones are the same root, which is a fair description of what the form does: it is the sentence shape that expects to be obeyed.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}habla\textquotedblright{} as a statement, then \textquotedblleft{}¡Habla!\textquotedblright{} as an order — same word, different job
  \item \textquotedblleft{}come\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}vive\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}
